AI News Tech United won’t let your AI agent book your flight AI agents can’t attest that you don’t have explosives in your bags.﻿ AI agents can’t attest that you don’t have explosives in your bags.﻿ by Lauren Feiner Nov 11, 2026, 9:54 PM UTC Link Share Gift If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.

See our ethics statement.

Photo by Daniel Karmann/picture alliance via Getty Images Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill.

She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

United says it won’t let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns.

The company says it hasn’t yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports , in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash .

But United is concerned that agents could expose customers’ information or make purchases they didn’t intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers — like having them attest that their bags don’t have explosives.

Related AI agents are causing massive headaches for banks. eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents While agents can still show users United flights, they won’t be able to actually complete the transaction on their behalf.

The decision, and others like it, could limit the potential usefulness of newer personal AI assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots . “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event on Tuesday, according to the Journal .

Across sectors, businesses are grappling with whether to let AI agents transact on their sites, and United is not alone in blocking access for unauthorized agents. eBay appeared to block agents from browsing the site, and several major banks have also placed restrictions on them.

United suggests it could reconsider its decision based on future advancements. “As third-party AI agents advance, we see the opportunities they present.

However, at the same time, allowing them to interact directly with a United account or booking could involve sensitive actions, and we want to make sure we have established protections for travelers first.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

articles.full_text:
11th November 2026 - Link Blog Anthropic's IPO roadshow video .

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper.

Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families.

That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy.

At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort.

Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build.

We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time.

In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out.

It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention .

Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers.

We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover.

Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger.

For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence.

A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model.

Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate.

They build on each other.

Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it.

They stack.

We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement.

Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

articles.title: Gemini Decisions API
articles.summary: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only.
articles.full_text:
11th November 2026 - Link Blog Gemini Decisions API ( via ) Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1".

This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.

It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free.

Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million.

Jev is text (and JSON) only.

OpenAI can handle text and images.

Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA?

Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } }
